rationale: Start with a broad, mid-temperature scouting gradient to elute all 10 compounds if possible and map the full elution window without risking truncation. This gives a good first read on whether peaks are compressed early, late, or across the gradient so later runs can trim the window and adjust slope.

All compounds eluted well within the gradient and the elution window is narrow, so trim the gradient to the observed phi range to reduce time while keeping peaks in-gradient. This should improve the time term and may also spread the mid-cluster slightly by focusing the gradient where the peaks actually elute.

The broad window was clearly faster and already fully resolved, so now test a steeper version to improve the time term while checking whether the critical mid-cluster remains adequately separated. This slope comparison will show how sensitive the worst pair is to gradient steepness and may already beat the current best.

The 10 min gradient is fastest but over-compresses the critical mid-cluster, while 20 min fully resolves it, so interpolate in slope to recover separation of peaks 5–7 with only a modest time penalty. This should improve the resolution term enough to beat the current best if that pair is slope-sensitive.

The limiting pair improves strongly with shallower slope: 10 min gave R 0.46, 14 min gave 1.20, and 20 min gave 2.36, so 16 min is the next logical refinement around the current optimum. It should further separate peaks 6–7 while likely keeping the run short enough to preserve a near-zero time penalty.

At 14 min the only remaining weakness is pair 6–7, and its strong dependence on slope suggests it is close enough that a modest temperature-selectivity shift could improve it without adding time penalty. Test a small decrease in T around the best method to see whether that critical pair opens while retaining the fast run.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity by collapsing peaks 5–6, so test the opposite direction from the current optimum. A modest increase to 45 C may reorder or open the critical central pair while preserving the favorable short runtime of the 14 min gradient.

Temperature changes both worsened the central selectivity, so the best remaining lever is fine adjustment of slope around the 14–16 min region. A 12 min run checks whether slightly steeper compression can still keep acceptable separation while improving the tradeoff enough to reveal where the true optimum lies.

All peaks elute well before the end of the gradient, with the last peak corresponding to only about phi_e ≈ 0.55, so the upper part of the 0.95 window is wasted. Narrowing phi1 while keeping tG and T fixed should make the effective gradient shallower in the occupied region and may open the critical 6–7 pair without increasing runtime much.

The improvement from phi1 0.95 to 0.85 shows the occupied gradient window was still broader than needed, so trim the upper end one more step while keeping the successful slope and temperature. This may further enhance separation of the critical central pair with only a small time increase, potentially improving on the current best.

The optimum in phi1 appears to lie between 0.85 and 0.95, with 0.85 best and 0.80 too slow, so test the other side of the bracket. This will localize the best gradient window around the current leader and show whether 0.85 is truly the sweet spot.

With phi1 = 0.90 outperforming both 0.85 and 0.95 at 14 min, the remaining opportunity is a slight shallowing of slope to improve the limiting 6–7 pair. Testing 16 min at this better-focused window may preserve full resolution while keeping the run short enough for a top CRF.

At phi1 = 0.90, 16 min is too slow and 14 min is excellent, so test the steeper side to bracket the optimum more tightly at this improved window. This will confirm whether 14 min is the local maximum or whether a shorter run can keep nearly the same resolution term with no time penalty.

The first peak is still fairly early, so raising phi0 one step while keeping the successful upper end and slope may trim dead space at the front and slightly compress the easy early region without sacrificing the critical central separation. This probes whether the lower edge of the gradient window can be tightened to improve the overall tradeoff beyond the current best.

Raising phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved CRF, so test one more step upward to see whether the lower gradient boundary can be tightened further around the actual elution window. This could shave early dead space and maintain the favorable central selectivity, but still keeps all peaks comfortably retained.

The best result came from tightening the lower boundary to phi0 = 0.10, while phi1 = 0.85 was also strong at phi0 = 0.05, so combine those two favorable window adjustments. This tests whether a slightly narrower, better-centered gradient can keep the zero time penalty and push the critical 6–7 pair just a bit more favorably.

You have already reached the maximum CRF, so preserve injection 16 as the incumbent and use remaining runs only to map robustness near it. Testing phi0 one step higher at the same successful phi1, tG, and T checks whether the optimum is broad or whether phi0 = 0.10 is a sharp sweet spot.

Two adjacent methods have now reached the maximum CRF, so continue defining the robust plateau by tightening the lower boundary one step further. This checks how far phi0 can be raised before the first peaks become too compressed or effectively unretained.

The maximum-CRF plateau includes phi0 = 0.10–0.15 at phi1 = 0.85, while phi1 = 0.80 was only tested with phi0 = 0.05. Test phi1 = 0.80 combined with the stronger phi0 = 0.10 setting to see whether this slightly narrower window also reaches the optimum.

Since both phi0 = 0.10 and 0.15 with phi1 = 0.85 reach CRF 1.000, test whether that robustness extends to the narrower upper bound phi1 = 0.80. This helps map the high-performing plateau and confirms whether phi1 = 0.85 is the true lower edge of the optimum region.

CRF is already maximal, so use the remaining runs to define the edge of the optimum by steepening the best window. This checks whether the successful phi0 = 0.10, phi1 = 0.85 method still stays on the CRF plateau at shorter tG, or whether 14 min is the minimum slope needed.

The 12 min version at phi0 = 0.10 fell off the optimum because the critical pair compressed, so test whether the equally optimal phi0 = 0.15 window tolerates the steeper gradient any better. This probes the shortest viable runtime within the proven high-performing plateau.

CRF is already maxed out, so use the remaining injections to assess robustness to temperature at the best window. A higher temperature previously altered central selectivity unfavorably at a broader window, and this run will show whether the optimized phi0/phi1 setting is more or less temperature-sensitive.

The optimized window at phi0 = 0.10, phi1 = 0.85 proved highly temperature-sensitive at 45 C, so test the alternate max-CRF method under the same temperature stress. This distinguishes whether the two optimal methods are equally robust or whether phi0 = 0.15 offers better tolerance.

Use the final run to complete the temperature-robustness bracket around the best method at 40 C. Since 45 C strongly collapsed the critical pair, this 35 C test will show whether the optimum is centered at 40 C or whether lower temperature is less damaging than higher temperature.
